title: Kernel switch exploration & nonblocking CUDA-graph diagnostics
summary: SE-led deep diagnostic session focused on kernel switching behavior during CUDA graph replay, nonblocking kernel paths, KV-cache priming effects, and end-to-end latency variability across TRT-LLM and vLLM execution paths on Asteria's on-prem cluster. Agreed next steps: run a controlled heatmap benchmark (scripts shared), capture cuda-gdb + nvprof traces, and schedule a 4-hour lab pairing session with Asteria's infra team next week.
action_items: Priya Shah: run provided heatmap benchmark across 1,2,4-gpu configurations and share raw csv (due 2029-11-19)
Carlos Ramos: attach example cudaGraph replay script + nvprof/nvtx wrappers into the shared drive (due 2029-11-14)
Evan Kato: enable kernel-level logging on on-prem cluster and grant temporary read to redwood-triage user (due 2029-11-15)
Maya Lee: send security whitepaper (SOC2/ISO) and check compliance Qs re: KMS in private deploy (due 2029-11-13)
next_steps: Run heatmap benchmark and upload results
Schedule 4-hour pairing lab w/ Redwood SEs (proposed 2029-11-20)
Share traces (cuda-gdb/nvprof) and a small repro with input prompts
Evaluate quantization knob (4-bit vs 8-bit) on a narrow prompt set for regressions
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2029-11-12
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~72 minutes
Attendees: Maya Lee, Carlos Ramos, Jia Patel (Redwood) — Priya Shah, Tom Nguyen, Evan Kato, Lina Alvarez (Asteria)

[00:00] Maya Lee (AE): All right, thanks everyone for joining. We'll hand over to Carlos for the deep dive, Carlos you wanna kick off?
[00:12] Carlos Ramos (SE): Yeah hi all. Quick agenda: first we'll walk through the probe harness we asked you to run, then dig into kernel switch events we've seen in your traces, and finally cover nonblocking cudagraph replay oddities and KV cache priming. Feel free to interrupt.
[00:28] Priya Shah (Customer): Sounds good. We ran the baseline scripts against two clusters — the 4-GPU NVLink rack and a 2-GPU isolated node — uploaded the csvs to the shared folder. There were a few outliers we couldn't explain, so hoping to get actionable items.
[00:44] Carlos Ramos (SE): Great, thanks. Quick note: I pulled the csvs — good to see both steady-state and warmstart runs. One high-level finding: when you replay cuda graphs with nonblocking launch (we call them NBL for short), we see kernel handoff frequency increase under sequence-length variance which triggers a kernel selection fallback about 6-7% of requests.
[01:03] Tom Nguyen (SRE): When you say fallback, you mean the runtime picks a different kernel implementation mid-inference?
[01:08] Carlos: Exactly. The runtime's kernel mapper prefers specialized TensorRT kernels for the common path (amortized batching), but when sequence length or KV cache hits shift, it swaps to a more conservative path — sometimes a vLLM-optimized op or a generic cuBLAS route. That swap has a short but visible latency penalty and sometimes invalidates cache assumptions leading to eviction thrash.
[01:28] Priya: We observed a 20–40 ms tail increase on some prompts, occasionally more. Is that the fallout?
[01:34] Carlos: Yeah, matches. The tail correlates with kernel switch events and with cudaGraph replay points where the graph capture included both blocking and nonblocking launches. Nonblocking launches can re-order kernels slightly, and if the kernel fingerprint changes the runtime falls back.
[01:50] Jia Patel (Redwood): To add, we've seen platform-specific heuristics that pick kernels based on tensor shapes, sequence length distribution, and whether KV cache is hot. On your NVLink cluster the cross-GPU eviction penalty is a big factor: when a KV page is evicted and needs to be fetched over NVLink it adds tens of ms which can push a request into a different execution lane.
[02:10] Evan Kato (Infra): On the NVLink rack, we do see occasional cross-socket RSVs — sometimes the peer-to-peer path is suboptimal due to PCIe topology; could that cause the longer fetch that flips a kernel choice?
[02:19] Carlos: Absolutely. If the data movement latency exceeds the runtime's threshold, kernel selection heuristics switch to safer kernels that avoid aggressive async copy patterns. Those safe kernels are slower on average but more deterministic.
[02:33] Priya: You mentioned eviction thrash — can you explain how that interacts with batching?
[02:38] Carlos: Sure. Continuous batching groups concurrent requests to improve throughput. But if the KV cache holds per-request primed state and an eviction happens mid-batch, some requests lose their local primer and must re-prime, which serializes parts of the batch. In practice we see this as both throughput drop and tail spikes.
[02:55] Tom: Is priming here the kv cache warming from previous tokens? We assumed our warmstart would eliminate those.
[03:00] Carlos: Warmstart helps, but priming is per-session. If you reuse sessions across requests but evictions occur due to limited cache memory or multi-tenant pressure, the warmstart benefit diminishes. Also quantized models use slightly different KV layout which can amplify eviction frequency.
[03:16] Priya: Right, we did trial 4-bit quant on a subset and saw more instability.
[03:20] Carlos: That's consistent — 4-bit quant packs tensors and changes memory alignment, sometimes triggering a different allocator path which interacts with the runtime's eviction policy. 8-bit tends to be safer in our experience for stability, though 4-bit wins on raw cost.
[03:34] Maya Lee (AE): From a product perspective this is a classic latency vs cost tradeoff — you get quant savings but potentially more tail and complexity in kernel routing.
[03:43] Priya: Understood. Back to CUDA graphs: you said nonblocking launch can reorder things. Is the recommendation to capture strictly blocking graphs?
[03:52] Carlos: It's nuanced. Blocking graphs are more deterministic but can be slower because they force sync points. Nonblocking graphs give better throughput but are sensitive to micro-timing differences. For on-prem with volatile NVLink topology, we recommend: 1) capture graphs at representative sequence distributions, 2) include a warm priming phase before capture, and 3) run a short randomized replay to detect kernel fingerprint shifts.
[04:16] Tom: What does a kernel fingerprint shift look like in the logs? We weren't sure which metric to watch.
[04:21] Carlos: You'll see a kernel id change in the runtime trace and an increase in kernel launch variance. Also nvtx ranges will jump — the stack will show different cuBLAS/TensorRT ops. We built a small parser that compares pre- and post-capture vbins and flags any mapping changes. I'll share that.
[04:39] Priya: You mentioned a heatmap earlier — what inputs do you want us to run?
[04:44] Carlos: The benchmark runs prompt-length sweep (8, 32, 64, 128), batch sizes (1,2,4,8), and two traffic shapes: steady and spike. We also toggle quantization and run capture/replay at each point. The output is a latency heatmap csv with kernel-switch counts.
[04:58] Priya: We already have something similar but with different capture cadence. We'll run your exact harness.
[05:03] Jia Patel: Perfect. Also capture nvprof timelines for the outliers — please include the full GPU timelines and nvtx ranges; that helps us spot queueing artifacts vs genuine kernel path swaps.
[05:15] Evan: On the cluster we have a current driver 535.x and CUDA 12.3 — any known interactions there?
[05:21] Carlos: Driver and CUDA can influence kernel selection only indirectly, but there were a few kernel variants introduced around CUDA 12.2 that change some heuristics. We'll check compatibility; if needed we can test a repro on our lab with 535 vs 540 driver.
[05:34] Lina (Head of ML): For the lab run, what's the minimum dataset of prompts you need? We want to limit PII and only run synthetic prompts.
[05:41] Carlos: Synthetic is fine; pick 50 diverse prompts covering short/long tail intents. Avoid user PII. The goal is shape, not content.
[05:48] Maya: Quick question for the infra team — are KMS/HSM policies going to block Redwood SE from pulling logs? Evan?
[05:54] Evan: We'll create a temporary read-only account that can access the logs folder — no KMS access needed for the raw GPU traces, but anything encrypted we will redact.
[06:04] Carlos: Thanks. One more nuance we saw: during CUDA graph replay, if an asynchronous memcpy (host->device) overlaps with another kernel's stream the runtime may pick a fallback kernel that assumes synchronous copy semantics. That subtle overlap is often missed in normal profiling.
[06:21] Tom: How can we detect that overlap?
[06:23] Carlos: NVTX timelines help — look for memcpy ranges that sit in the same stream as compute but without explicit stream sync. Also our parser checks stream ids and notes if memcpy and kernel overlap windows exceed X ms. We'll hand over the parser.
[06:37] Priya: A question about vLLM — in some of our runs vllm path looked massively faster for batch=8 but worse for batch=1. Does that track with expected behavior?
[06:46] Carlos: Yes: vLLM favors dynamic batching and is optimized for CPU+CUDA hybrid pipelines in some deploys. It shines when you can aggregate many concurrent requests. TensorRT-LLM optimized kernels are better at single-request latency when the kernel is specialized. That's why you saw the crossover. Kernel selection tries to pick the best path but when traffic oscillates quickly, it may flip and cause extra tail.
[07:05] Priya: So for user-facing low-latency features we should bias toward specialized TRT kernels and limit batching?
[07:11] Jia: Or set lane policies: reserve a lane for low-latency requests pinned to TRT path, and a separate lane for bulk throughput that can use vLLM or more aggressive quant. Redwood's routing supports that kind of per-route policy.
[07:22] Evan: That might fit our product requirements. We'll need docs on configuring lanes and autoscale interplay.
[07:28] Maya: I'll include a configuration exemplar in the notes.
[07:32] [08:00] — 20-minute silent debug segment summary omitted —
[27:35] Carlos: We dug into a specific evicted trace: sequence length was 128, batch 4, quant=4-bit, and on replay the runtime swapped to the safe kernel due to an async memcpy overlapping with the cache fetch. The extra NVLink hop added ~48ms on that request.
[27:50] Priya: That sounds like our CSV outlier. The stack trace we saw shows an unusual memcpy at 01:22:33.
[27:57] Carlos: Exactly. We annotated those ranges in your file.
[28:02] Tom: Any mitigation short-term? We can avoid 4-bit for now and try 8-bit and retest.
[28:07] Carlos: Yes 8-bit + forcing blocking capture for graphs reduced kernel switches in our lab runs. It won't be as performant as a perfect nonblocking graph, but it reduced tail by about 30–50% on similar racks.
[28:20] Priya: How about forcing a particular kernel? Is that exposed?
[28:24] Carlos: There are runtime flags to prefer a kernel family or disable certain optimizer passes. We can share a sandbox config. Use with caution — you may lose some throughput.
[28:34] Priya: Understood.
[28:36] Jia: Another low-level tool we use is a randomized fuzz of sequence variations during capture to ensure the captured graph generalizes. It can reveal fragile paths.
[28:47] Evan: We'll run that too.
[28:50] Priya: Any notes on memory fragmentation with quantized models? We had a few OOM-like evictions even though apparent usage was under threshold.
[28:58] Carlos: Fragmentation is real — quant packing and alignment can leave small unusable gaps. Runtime allocators sometimes move to slower alloc paths that appear as extra latency. Running a compacting allocator or preallocating a slab for KV pages helps. We'll send recommendations.
[29:13] Maya: Let's recap next steps quickly. Priya runs heatmap bench, Evan enables logs and shares access, Carlos will share the parser and mvprof/nvtx wrapper, Maya will share compliance docs and lane config example.
[29:28] Priya: Good. Also can we schedule the 4-hour lab? We prefer next Wednesday.
[29:33] Maya: I'll propose slots for 2029-11-20 in the follow-up email.
[29:38] Tom: One last operational Q: if we see persistent kernel switching in production, what's Redwood's recommended escalation?
[29:44] Carlos: Raise a ticket with the KERNEL-SWAP priority; attach the heatmap and nvprof traces. Our SEs will triage and, if needed, open a lab-blast where we run targeted microbenchmarks in our infra.
[29:58] Priya: Great. Thanks everyone.
[30:02] Maya: Thanks all — we'll follow up with artifacts and calendar invites.

End of transcript. Note: transcript contains some auto-corrected names and occasional mis-attributions typical of Fireflies export.
